_comment: Authored, server-gradable GATE-standard practice items for the decompositions
cluster of linear algebra: orthogonality, Gram-Schmidt, quadratic forms,
positive definite matrices, SVD, least squares, and matrix norms.
Every item was solved by hand (twice, via independent methods where
possible — e.g. direct multiplication vs. characteristic-polynomial factoring,
or Sylvester's criterion vs. explicit eigenvalue signs) before its key was
written. Matrices are chosen with clean integer or simple-fraction values so
a student (or a reviewer) can re-derive every answer by hand.
Shape mirrors gate-ma-linear-algebra.json exactly (same AuthoredItem schema

items.question_text: Which of the following matrices is orthogonal (QᵀQ = I)?
solution_steps: [[1,1],[1,1]] is singular (columns are identical, not even linearly independent), so it cannot be orthogonal.

items.question_text: Find the scalar t such that the projection of b = (3, 4) onto a = (1, 2) equals t·a.
solution_steps: The scalar projection coefficient formula is t = (a·b)/(a·a).

items.question_text: Which of the following statements about orthogonal matrices Q are true?
options: Q satisfies QᵀQ = QQᵀ = I
The columns of Q form an orthonormal set
The determinant of an orthogonal matrix is always +1
Orthogonal matrices preserve vector lengths: ‖Qx‖ = ‖x‖ for every x
The inverse of an orthogonal matrix equals its transpose
solution_steps: (a),(e) TRUE: QᵀQ=I is the defining property, and it directly implies Q⁻¹ = Qᵀ (and then QQᵀ=I follows too, since Q⁻¹Q=I means QQ⁻¹=I also, i.e. QQᵀ=I).
(b) TRUE: QᵀQ=I written entry-wise says (column i)·(column j) = δᵢⱼ, i.e. columns are unit length and pairwise orthogonal — orthonormal.
(c) FALSE: det(Q)² = det(Qᵀ)det(Q) = det(QᵀQ) = det(I) = 1, so det(Q) = ±1, not always +1 — a reflection matrix like [[1,0],[0,-1]] is orthogonal with determinant -1.
(d) TRUE: ‖Qx‖² = (Qx)ᵀ(Qx) = xᵀQᵀQx = xᵀIx = xᵀx = ‖x‖².

items.question_text: Using Gram-Schmidt on v1 = (1,1), v2 = (1,0), with u1 = v1, what is u2 (before normalization)?
solution_steps: u2 = v2 - proj_{u1}(v2), where proj_{u1}(v2) = (u1·v2 / u1·u1)·u1.
Check orthogonality: u1·u2 = 1·0.5 + 1·(-0.5) = 0.5-0.5 = 0 — confirmed orthogonal to u1.

items.question_text: Continuing from u2 = (0.5, -0.5) (the second Gram-Schmidt vector for v1=(1,1), v2=(1,0)), find the x-component of the normalized vector e2 = u2/‖u2‖.
solution_steps: The x-component is ≈ 0.7071 (= 1/√2).
Check: e2 should be a unit vector — 0.7071² + 0.7071² ≈ 0.5+0.5 = 1 — confirmed.

items.question_text: Gram-Schmidt applied to a linearly independent set {v1,...,vn} produces an orthonormal set {e1,...,en} such that...
options: span{e1,...,ek} = span{v1,...,vk} for every k from 1 to n
eₖ is a linear combination of v1,...,vn (all n vectors) for every k
the eᵢ's need not be unit vectors
the process changes the span of the whole set {v1,...,vn}
solution_steps: By construction, u_k = v_k minus its projections onto u1,...,u_{k-1}, so u_k (and hence e_k) is a combination of v_1,...,v_k ONLY — never later vectors v_{k+1},...,v_n.
This means span{e1,...,ek} = span{u1,...,uk} = span{v1,...,vk} at every intermediate step k, which is exactly what makes Gram-Schmidt useful for building nested orthonormal bases.

The 'orthoNORMAL' in Gram-Schmidt specifically requires each eᵢ to be normalized to unit length, and the overall span of the full set {e1,...,en} equals span{v1,...,vn} unchanged — only the basis representation changes, not the subspace.

items.question_text: v1 = (1,0,0), v2 = (1,1,0), v3 = (1,1,2). Apply Gram-Schmidt; find ‖u3‖ (the norm of the third orthogonal vector, before normalization).
solution_steps: Check: u1, u2, u3 are pairwise orthogonal (dot products all 0), and u1+u2+u3 = (1,0,0)+(0,1,0)+(0,0,2) = (1,1,2) = v3 — confirmed the reconstruction is consistent.

items.question_text: Which of the following statements about Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization are true?
options: Applying Gram-Schmidt to the columns of a matrix A produces the Q factor of the QR decomposition A = QR
The resulting orthonormal vectors depend on the order in which the original vectors are processed
Gram-Schmidt requires the input vectors to already be orthogonal
If the input vectors are linearly dependent, the process produces a zero vector at some step
The output of Gram-Schmidt is always identical regardless of the ordering of the input vectors
items.correct_answer: Produces Q in QR decomposition; order-dependent output; dependent inputs yield a zero vector at some step
solution_steps: (a) TRUE: this is exactly how the QR decomposition is constructed — Q's columns are the Gram-Schmidt orthonormal vectors, and R records the projection coefficients.

(b) TRUE and (e) FALSE: reordering v1,...,vn generally changes which subspaces span{v1,...,vk} the process is forced to match at each step, so a different order gives a genuinely different orthonormal basis (though it still spans the same overall space).
(c) FALSE: Gram-Schmidt is specifically designed to work on any linearly INDEPENDENT (not necessarily orthogonal) set — that's the whole point of the algorithm.
(d) TRUE: if v_k is a linear combination of v_1,...,v_{k-1}, then subtracting off all its projections onto u_1,...,u_{k-1} leaves exactly the zero vector at step k.

items.question_text: The quadratic form Q(x,y) = 2x² + 4xy + 3y² corresponds to xᵀAx for which symmetric matrix A?
solution_steps: For A=[[a,b],[b,c]], xᵀAx = a·x² + 2b·xy + c·y².

Matching coefficients: a=2 (x² coefficient), c=3 (y² coefficient), and 2b = 4 (xy coefficient) so b=2 — the off-diagonal entry is HALF the xy-coefficient, since it's counted twice (once as (1,2), once as (2,1)).
So A = [[2,2],[2,3]]. Check: xᵀAx = 2x² + 2xy + 2xy + 3y² = 2x² + 4xy + 3y² — matches Q exactly.
The wrong option [[2,4],[4,3]] is the classic error of using the full xy-coefficient as the off-diagonal entry instead of splitting it in half.

items.question_text: Classify the quadratic form Q(x,y) = 2x² + 4xy + 3y² (matrix A = [[2,2],[2,3]]).
options: Positive definite
Negative definite
Indefinite
Positive semidefinite
solution_steps: Leading principal minors of A: D1 = 2 > 0. D2 = det(A) = 2·3 - 2·2 = 6-4 = 2 > 0.
By Sylvester's criterion, all leading principal minors positive means A is positive definite.

Cross-check via eigenvalues: trace=5, det=2, characteristic equation λ²-5λ+2=0 has roots λ=(5±√17)/2 — since the sum (5) and product (2) are both positive, both roots must be positive, confirming positive definiteness.

items.question_text: For Q(x,y,z) = x² + 2y² + 3z² + 2xy, the matrix is A = [[1,1,0],[1,2,0],[0,0,3]]. Find D3, the determinant of A (the third leading principal minor).
solution_steps: A is block diagonal: the top-left 2x2 block [[1,1],[1,2]] and the 1x1 block [3], since the z row/column has no interaction with x,y.
det of a block-diagonal matrix is the product of the block determinants: det([[1,1],[1,2]]) = 1·2-1·1 = 1, and det([3]) = 3.
Cross-check via cofactor expansion along the third row: det(A) = 3·det([[1,1],[1,2]]) - 0 + 0 = 3·1 = 3 — matches.

items.question_text: For which range of the real parameter t is Q(x,y) = x² + 2txy + 4y² positive definite?
options: t² < 2
solution_steps: The matrix is A = [[1,t],[t,4]]. Leading principal minors: D1 = 1 > 0 for all t (always satisfied).
D2 = det(A) = 1·4 - t·t = 4 - t². For positive definiteness we need D2 > 0, i.e. 4 - t² > 0, i.e. t² < 4.
t² < 4 is equivalent to -2 < t < 2.
Check a boundary case: at t=2, D2 = 4-4 = 0, so A is only positive SEMIdefinite there (eigenvalue 0 appears), confirming the strict inequality -2<t<2 (not ≤) is required for positive definiteness.

items.question_text: Which of the following statements about quadratic forms xᵀAx (A symmetric) are true?
options: xᵀAx is positive definite iff all eigenvalues of A are positive
xᵀAx is positive semidefinite iff all eigenvalues of A are non-negative
Sylvester's criterion requires checking only the determinant of the full matrix A
An indefinite quadratic form has both positive and negative eigenvalues
Every quadratic form xᵀAx can be classified using only the trace of A
items.correct_answer: PD iff all eigenvalues positive; PSD iff all eigenvalues non-negative; indefinite has mixed-sign eigenvalues
solution_steps: (a),(b) TRUE: since A=QΛQᵀ, xᵀAx = (Qᵀx)ᵀΛ(Qᵀx) = Σλᵢyᵢ² where y=Qᵀx ranges over all of ℝⁿ as x does — this sum is always positive (or non-negative) exactly when every λᵢ is positive (or non-negative).

(c) FALSE: Sylvester's criterion requires ALL leading principal minors D1, D2, ..., Dn to be positive, not just the full determinant Dn — pi-quadratic-forms-003's block matrix would need D1 and D2 checked too, not just D3.
(d) TRUE: by the same Σλᵢyᵢ² decomposition, mixing a positive and a negative eigenvalue lets the form take both positive and negative values.

(e) FALSE: trace only gives the sum of eigenvalues, which is not enough to determine their individual signs — e.g. trace=1 is consistent with eigenvalues (2,-1) [indefinite] or (0.5,0.5) [positive semidefinite].

items.question_text: Is A = [[4, 2], [2, 3]] positive definite?
options: Yes — both leading principal minors (4 and 8) are positive
Yes — because its diagonal entries (4 and 3) are positive
No — off-diagonal entries are nonzero
No — the determinant test only applies to diagonal matrices
items.correct_answer: Yes — both leading principal minors (4 and 8) are positive
solution_steps: By Sylvester's criterion, both leading principal minors positive means A is positive definite.

Option (b)'s reasoning is a common trap: positive diagonal entries alone do NOT guarantee positive definiteness — see pi-positive-definite-matrices-003 for a counterexample where diagonal entries are positive but the matrix is not positive definite.

items.question_text: A = [[5, 2], [2, 2]] is positive definite. Find its smallest eigenvalue.
solution_steps: Characteristic equation: λ² - 7λ + 6 = 0, which factors as (λ-6)(λ-1) = 0, giving eigenvalues 6 and 1.
Both eigenvalues (6, 1) are positive, confirming A is positive definite (consistent with D1=5>0, D2=6>0 via Sylvester's criterion).
The smallest eigenvalue is 1.

items.question_text: Is A = [[1, 2], [2, 1]] positive definite?
options: No — the second leading principal minor is -3 < 0
Yes — diagonal entries are positive
No — the matrix is not symmetric
Yes — trace is positive
items.correct_answer: No — the second leading principal minor is -3 < 0
solution_steps: Since not all leading principal minors are positive, A is NOT positive definite (Sylvester's criterion fails at D2).

Cross-check via eigenvalues: trace=2, det=-3, characteristic equation λ²-2λ-3=0 factors as (λ-3)(λ+1)=0, giving eigenvalues 3 and -1 — mixed signs mean A is actually indefinite, confirming it is not positive definite.
A IS symmetric (the (1,2) and (2,1) entries both equal 2), so option (c)'s reasoning is factually wrong even though positive diagonal entries alone (option b) are also insufficient.

items.question_text: A = [[4, 2], [2, 3]] is positive definite. Its Cholesky decomposition is A = LLᵀ with L = [[l11, 0], [l21, l22]]. Find l22.
solution_steps: Check by reconstructing LLᵀ: L = [[2,0],[1,√2]], LLᵀ = [[2,0],[1,√2]]·[[2,1],[0,√2]] = [[4, 2],[2, 1+2]] = [[4,2],[2,3]] — matches A exactly, confirming the Cholesky decomposition.

items.question_text: Which of the following statements about positive definite matrices are true?
options: All eigenvalues of a positive definite matrix are strictly positive
A positive definite matrix is always invertible
The determinant of a positive definite matrix is always positive
A positive definite matrix can have a zero entry on its diagonal
Every symmetric matrix with positive diagonal entries is positive definite
items.correct_answer: Eigenvalues strictly positive; always invertible; determinant always positive
solution_steps: (a) TRUE by definition (or equivalently, xᵀAx>0 for all x≠0 forces every eigenvalue positive, taking x to be an eigenvector).
(b) TRUE: since 0 is never an eigenvalue (all eigenvalues > 0), det(A) = product of eigenvalues ≠ 0, so A is invertible.
(c) TRUE: det(A) equals the product of the (all positive) eigenvalues, which is itself positive.

(d) FALSE: the (i,i) diagonal entry of A equals eᵢᵀAeᵢ where eᵢ is the i-th standard basis vector; positive definiteness requires this to be strictly positive for every i, so no diagonal entry can be zero.
(e) FALSE: pi-positive-definite-matrices-003's A=[[1,2],[2,1]] has positive diagonal entries (1,1) but is not positive definite (D2=-3<0) — a direct counterexample.

items.question_text: The singular values of a matrix A are related to the eigenvalues of AᵀA by which formula?
options: σᵢ = √(λᵢ), where λᵢ are eigenvalues of AᵀA
σᵢ = λᵢ
σᵢ = λᵢ²
σᵢ = 1/λᵢ
items.correct_answer: σᵢ = √(λᵢ), where λᵢ are eigenvalues of AᵀA
solution_steps: AᵀA is symmetric positive semidefinite, so its eigenvalues λᵢ are always ≥ 0.
By definition, the singular values of A are the (non-negative) square roots of the eigenvalues of AᵀA: σᵢ = √λᵢ.
This is well-defined precisely because AᵀA's eigenvalues are never negative, so the square root is always real.

items.question_text: A = [[2, 2], [1, 1]]. Find the largest singular value of A (i.e. √λ_max of AᵀA).
solution_steps: trace(AᵀA) = 10, det(AᵀA) = 25-25 = 0, so the characteristic equation λ²-10λ = 0 gives eigenvalues λ = 10, 0.
The largest singular value is σ_max = √10 ≈ 3.1623.
Cross-check: A's rows are proportional (row1 = 2·row2), so rank(A) = 1, consistent with exactly one nonzero singular value (√10) and one zero singular value.

items.question_text: By the Eckart-Young theorem, the best rank-1 approximation (in Frobenius norm) of a matrix A is obtained by...
options: keeping only the largest singular value term σ1·u1v1ᵀ and discarding the rest of the SVD sum
averaging all the singular value terms
keeping only the smallest singular value term
rounding all entries of A to the nearest integer
items.correct_answer: keeping only the largest singular value term σ1·u1v1ᵀ
solution_steps: Writing the full SVD as A = Σᵢ σᵢ uᵢvᵢᵀ (sorted so σ1 ≥ σ2 ≥ ... ≥ 0), the Eckart-Young theorem states that truncating this sum to its first k terms gives the best rank-k approximation to A in Frobenius (and spectral) norm.
For k=1, that means keeping only the σ1·u1v1ᵀ term — the direction of largest 'stretch' — and discarding the rest.
This is the theoretical basis for low-rank compression / denoising via SVD.

items.question_text: A = [[2, 2], [1, 1]] has singular values √10 and 0. Compute ‖A‖_F² (the squared Frobenius norm) using its singular values.
solution_steps: A key SVD identity: ‖A‖_F² = Σᵢ σᵢ², the sum of the squared singular values.
Cross-check by direct computation: ‖A‖_F² = sum of squares of all entries = 2²+2²+1²+1² = 4+4+1+1 = 10 — matches exactly.

items.question_text: Which of the following statements about the singular value decomposition (SVD) are true?
options: The singular values of A are the square roots of the eigenvalues of AᵀA (equivalently of AAᵀ)
The number of nonzero singular values equals rank(A)
SVD applies only to square matrices
The largest singular value equals the spectral (2-norm) norm of A
U and V in A = UΣVᵀ are always the same matrix
items.correct_answer: Singular values from AᵀA eigenvalues; count = rank; largest singular value = spectral norm
solution_steps: (a) TRUE by definition (see pi-svd-001); AᵀA and AAᵀ always share the same nonzero eigenvalues.
(b) TRUE: pi-svd-002's rank-1 matrix has exactly one nonzero singular value (√10), matching rank(A)=1.
(c) FALSE: SVD is defined for ANY m×n matrix, square or rectangular — this generality is one of its main advantages over eigendecomposition.
(d) TRUE: ‖A‖₂ = max_{‖x‖=1} ‖Ax‖ = σ_max, the largest singular value, by definition of the spectral (operator 2-) norm.

(e) FALSE: U (left singular vectors, eigenvectors of AAᵀ) and V (right singular vectors, eigenvectors of AᵀA) are generally different matrices, and even have different dimensions when A is rectangular.

items.question_text: For an overdetermined system Ax = b with no exact solution, the least-squares solution x̂ satisfies which equation?
options: AᵀA x̂ = Aᵀb
A x̂ = b
AAᵀ x̂ = b
Aᵀ x̂ = Aᵀb
solution_steps: The least-squares solution minimizes ‖Ax-b‖², and setting the gradient of this quadratic to zero gives the normal equations AᵀAx = Aᵀb.
This is solvable for x̂ whenever A has full column rank (so AᵀA is invertible): x̂ = (AᵀA)⁻¹Aᵀb.
Ax=b generally has no solution (that's the whole premise of 'overdetermined'), so it is not what x̂ satisfies exactly.

items.question_text: Fit y = mx + c by least squares to the points (0,1), (1,3), (2,4). Find the slope m.
solution_steps: Cross-check with the standard slope formula: with n=3, Σx=3, Σy=8, Σxy=11, Σx²=5, m = (nΣxy - ΣxΣy)/(nΣx² - (Σx)²) = (3·11-3·8)/(3·5-9) = (33-24)/6 = 1.5 — matches.
The slope is 1.5.

items.question_text: Continuing the least-squares fit y = mx + c to (0,1), (1,3), (2,4) (with m = 1.5 from AᵀAx̂=Aᵀb), find the intercept c.
solution_steps: From the same solve as pi-least-squares-002: c = (5·8-3·11)/6 = (40-33)/6 = 7/6 ≈ 1.16667.
Cross-check with the standard formula: c = (Σy - mΣx)/n = (8 - 1.5·3)/3 = (8-4.5)/3 = 3.5/3 = 7/6 — matches.
So the least-squares line is y = 1.5x + 7/6.

items.question_text: Using the least-squares fit y = 1.5x + 7/6 to (0,1), (1,3), (2,4), compute the sum of the three residuals rᵢ = yᵢ - ŷᵢ.
solution_steps: This is not a coincidence: the normal equations AᵀAx̂=Aᵀb guarantee the residual vector r=b-Ax̂ is orthogonal to every column of A, and here the first column of A is all 1's — so the residuals must sum to exactly zero.

items.question_text: Which of the following statements about least-squares solutions are true?
options: The least-squares solution minimizes ‖Ax-b‖₂, the Euclidean norm of the residual
The normal equations AᵀAx=Aᵀb always have a solution when A has full column rank
The residual vector b-Ax̂ is always orthogonal to the column space of A
Least squares requires the system Ax=b to be square (same number of equations as unknowns)
If A has full column rank, then AᵀA is invertible
items.correct_answer: Minimizes residual norm; solvable with full column rank; residual orthogonal to col(A); AᵀA invertible with full column rank
solution_steps: (a) TRUE: this is the definition of the least-squares problem.
(b) TRUE and (e) TRUE: full column rank means AᵀA is invertible (a symmetric positive definite matrix), so x̂=(AᵀA)⁻¹Aᵀb always exists and is unique.
(c) TRUE: the normal equations AᵀAx̂=Aᵀb rearrange to Aᵀ(b-Ax̂)=0, meaning the residual is orthogonal to every column of A, i.e. to all of col(A) — verified numerically in pi-least-squares-004.
(d) FALSE: least squares is specifically designed for OVERDETERMINED systems (more equations/rows than unknowns/columns), like the 3-equations-2-unknowns line fit above.

items.question_text: A = [[3, 4], [0, 0]]. Find the Frobenius norm ‖A‖_F.
solution_steps: ‖A‖_F = √(Σ over all entries of aᵢⱼ²) = √(3² + 4² + 0² + 0²) = √(9+16) = √25 = 5.

items.question_text: A = [[1, -2], [3, 4]]. What is ‖A‖₁ (the maximum absolute column sum)?
solution_steps: ‖A‖₁ = max over columns of the sum of absolute values in that column.
The maximum is 6 (from column 2).

items.question_text: A = [[2, -3, 1], [0, 4, -1], [5, 0, 2]]. Find ‖A‖∞ (the maximum absolute row sum).
solution_steps: ‖A‖∞ = max over rows of the sum of absolute values in that row.
The maximum is 7 (from row 3).

items.question_text: A = [[4, 0], [3, 5]]. Find the 2-norm condition number κ₂(A) = σ_max/σ_min.
solution_steps: trace(AᵀA) = 50, det(AᵀA) = 625-225 = 400. Characteristic equation λ²-50λ+400=0, discriminant = 2500-1600=900, √900=30, so λ = (50±30)/2 = 40 or 10.

Cross-check using AAᵀ instead (same nonzero eigenvalues guaranteed for square A): AAᵀ = [[4,0],[3,5]]·[[4,3],[0,5]] = [[16,12],[12,34]], trace=50, det=16·34-12·12=544-144=400 — same trace and det, confirming eigenvalues 40, 10 and κ₂(A)=2.

items.question_text: Which of the following statements about matrix norms and condition numbers are true?
options: The Frobenius norm ‖A‖_F equals the square root of the sum of squares of all entries of A
The condition number κ(A) = ‖A‖‖A⁻¹‖ is always ≥ 1
A matrix with a large condition number is said to be well-conditioned
For a symmetric matrix, ‖A‖₂ equals the largest absolute eigenvalue of A
The 1-norm of a matrix is the maximum absolute row sum
items.correct_answer: Frobenius norm formula; condition number ≥1; symmetric matrix 2-norm = largest |eigenvalue|
solution_steps: (a) TRUE: this is the defining formula, verified numerically in pi-matrix-norms-001.
(b) TRUE: κ(A) = ‖A‖‖A⁻¹‖ ≥ ‖AA⁻¹‖ = ‖I‖ = 1, by the submultiplicative property of induced matrix norms.
(c) FALSE: a LARGE condition number means A is ILL-conditioned (sensitive to small perturbations in input); a condition number near 1 means well-conditioned.
(d) TRUE: for symmetric A, singular values equal |eigenvalues| (since A²'s eigenvalues are eigenvalues² of A), so the largest singular value (=‖A‖₂) is the largest |eigenvalue|.
(e) FALSE: the 1-norm is the maximum absolute COLUMN sum (see pi-matrix-norms-002); the maximum absolute row sum is the ∞-norm (see pi-matrix-norms-003) — these are commonly swapped by mistake.
